procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (implied, as the case involves committal to the Court of Sessions)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 10th July, 1975 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Misc. No. 1104 of 1975, granting bail to the respondents.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Allahabad High Court granted bail to the respondents on the grounds that they could not be remanded to custody before an order committing them to the Court of Sessions was made. The High Court undertook an investigation of a point of law which did not directly arise in the facts before the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of U.P. appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court initially questioned the utility of the appeal, as the trial might have concluded. However, the Court proceeded to hear the appeal because the High Court's interpretation of sections 207, 209, and 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure could lead to miscarriage of justice in other cases by introducing a stage of compulsory bail not warranted by the Code. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order granting bail, but noted that if the trial was over, the order would have no effect.

directions: The order of the High Court granting bail to the respondents on the short ground that they could not be remanded to the custody before the order committing them to the Court of Sessions is made, is set aside.
If in the meantime, the trial is over, no question of taking the respondents into custody pursuant to the order would arise.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate has the jurisdiction to remand an accused to custody after a police report (chargesheet) is filed but before an order of commitment is made under Section 209 Cr.P.C. in a case exclusively triable by the Court of Sessions.

facts: A police report (chargesheet) has been filed before a Magistrate for an offence that is exclusively triable by a Court of Sessions.
The accused has been produced before the Magistrate.
The Magistrate has taken cognizance of the offence but has not yet made an order committing the case to the Court of Sessions under Section 209 Cr.P.C.
law: Section 207 Cr.P.C.: Mandates the Magistrate to supply copies of police reports and other documents to the accused.
Section 209 Cr.P.C.: Empowers the Magistrate to commit the case to the Court of Sessions and, subject to bail provisions, remand the accused to custody during and until the conclusion of the trial.
Section 309(2) Cr.P.C.: Allows a court, after taking cognizance, to postpone or adjourn any 'enquiry' or 'trial' and remand the accused to custody during the adjournment.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view that the Magistrate's function between taking cognizance and committing the case is not an 'enquiry'.
The Court held that the Magistrate's duty to ensure compliance with Section 207 (supplying documents) is a judicial function and constitutes an 'enquiry' under the Code.
Because these proceedings are an 'enquiry', the Magistrate can exercise the power under Section 309(2) to adjourn the proceedings and remand the accused to custody.

The Court reasoned that the High Court's interpretation would lead to an absurd and untenable result: a 'compulsory bail' stage not intended by the law, where a Magistrate would be forced to release an accused simply because the procedural steps for commitment were not yet complete.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a Magistrate has the jurisdiction and power, derived from Section 309(2) Cr.P.C., to remand an accused to custody during the period after a chargesheet is filed and before an order of commitment is made under Section 209. The High Court's contrary view was set aside as 'wholly untenable'.

issue.issue_text: Whether the proceedings before a Magistrate after the submission of a chargesheet and until the commitment of the case to the Court of Sessions (including functions under Sections 207 and 209 Cr.P.C.) constitute an "inquiry" for the purposes of Section 309(2) Cr.P.C., thereby empowering the Magistrate to remand the accused to custody.

facts: The case concerned the power of a Magistrate to remand an accused to custody after a chargesheet has been filed but before the case is formally committed to the Court of Sessions.

The High Court had ruled that the Magistrate's functions during this period, specifically under Sections 207 (supplying copies of documents to the accused) and 209 (committing the case) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), were not an "inquiry."
According to the High Court, since these proceedings were not an inquiry, the Magistrate lacked the power under Section 309(2) Cr.P.C. to remand the accused to custody.
law: Section 2(g) of the Cr.P.C. defines an "inquiry" as every inquiry, other than a trial, conducted under the Code by a Magistrate or Court.
Section 207 of the Cr.P.C. requires the Magistrate to ensure that the accused is furnished with copies of the police report and other relevant documents.
Section 209 of the Cr.P.C. outlines the procedure for committing a case to the Court of Sessions when the offence is exclusively triable by it.
Section 309(2) of the Cr.P.C. empowers a court, after taking cognizance of an offence, to postpone or adjourn an "inquiry" or trial and remand the accused to custody during such postponement.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view that the Magistrate's role was merely administrative. It held that the function of ensuring compliance with Section 207 is a judicial function.

The Court reasoned that the Magistrate must apply their mind to ascertain whether the required documents have been supplied to the accused. This process of ascertainment and achieving "judicial satisfaction" is not a trial, but it is a judicial proceeding, and therefore falls squarely within the definition of an "inquiry."

The Court further clarified that the entire process—from the moment the accused is produced with the chargesheet, through the compliance with Section 207, and culminating in the commitment order under Section 209—constitutes a single, continuous inquiry.

Since these proceedings were established to be an "inquiry," the Court found that Section 309(2) Cr.P.C. was directly applicable. This section explicitly grants the Magistrate the authority to remand an accused to custody if it becomes necessary to adjourn the inquiry for any reason (such as the documents not being ready).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the proceedings before a Magistrate after the submission of a chargesheet and until the commitment of the case to the Court of Sessions (including functions under Sections 207 and 209 Cr.P.C.) do constitute an "inquiry." Consequently, the Magistrate is empowered by Section 309(2) Cr.P.C. to remand the accused to custody during this period.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate has the jurisdiction to remand an accused to custody after a police report (chargesheet) is filed but before an order of commitment is made under Section 209 Cr.P.C. in a case exclusively triable by the Court of Sessions.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's interpretation of the law is incorrect and creates a stage of compulsory bail for persons accused of serious offenses, which is not warranted by the Criminal Procedure Code.
This interpretation is likely to result in a miscarriage of justice in a large number of cases, as individuals who would not otherwise be entitled to discretionary bail would be released.
respondent_arguments: The respondents did not appear at the hearing. Their argument is reflected in the High Court's ruling, which held that an accused could not be remanded to custody after a chargesheet is filed but before the case is committed to the Court of Sessions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the proceedings before a Magistrate after the submission of a chargesheet and until the commitment of the case to the Court of Sessions (including functions under Sections 207 and 209 Cr.P.C.) constitute an "inquiry" for the purposes of Section 309(2) Cr.P.C., thereby empowering the Magistrate to remand the accused to custody.
appellant_arguments: The proceedings before the Magistrate after the submission of the police report, including functions under Sections 207 and 209, constitute an "inquiry" under the Code.
Because these proceedings are an inquiry, Section 309(2) of the Code empowers the Magistrate to remand the accused to custody while the inquiry is pending completion.
respondent_arguments: The respondents did not appear at the hearing. Their argument is reflected in the High Court's ruling, which implicitly held that the functions of a Magistrate under Section 207 are not a judicial function and do not constitute an "inquiry" as contemplated by the Code, thus precluding the use of remand powers under Section 309(2).

cases.case_name: State of Bihar and Anr. v. J.A.C. Saldanha and Ors.
cases.principle: The text states this case was 'referred to' but does not specify the legal principle for which the Supreme Court relied on it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The proceedings before a Magistrate, which take place after a police report is submitted and before an order of commitment to the Court of Sessions is made, constitute an 'inquiry'. Therefore, under Section 309(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a Magistrate has the authority to remand an accused to custody during this period.
obiter: It is futile for a High Court to undertake an investigation of a point of law which does not directly arise from the facts before it, as courts should ordinarily not undertake academic exercises.

On the expiry of 60 days from the date of arrest, if a charge-sheet is not submitted, an accused is entitled to be released on bail if they apply for it; however, if they do not apply, their continued detention is not ipso facto illegal or without the authority of law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The function discharged by a Magistrate under Section 207 of the Cr.P.C. (ensuring copies of documents are furnished to the accused) after a police report is filed is a judicial function, not a mere administrative task. Because this function is judicial in nature and is not a trial, it constitutes an "inquiry" as contemplated by the Code. This inquiry period extends from the time the accused is produced with the police report until the Magistrate makes the order of commitment under Section 209. Consequently, Section 309(2) of the Code empowers the Magistrate to remand the accused to custody during this pending inquiry, and the High Court's view that the Magistrate lacks such jurisdiction is wholly untenable.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a proceeding before a Magistrate is a "judicial function" that is "something other than a trial." If so, the proceeding constitutes an "inquiry" for the purposes of the Criminal Procedure Code, thereby triggering the remand powers available under Section 309(2).
policy_considerations: The High Court's interpretation introduces a "stage of 'compulsory bail' not envisaged by the Code," which is an untenable outcome.

Allowing the High Court's view to stand would create a legal vacuum where a Magistrate would have no jurisdiction to remand an accused after the chargesheet is filed but before commitment, forcing a situation where the Magistrate must either grant bail or commit the case forthwith, which is not the scheme of the Code.
